Q: Git case-sensitive filename issue on macOS causing duplicate files and deployment failures on Linux A:

This happens because macOS is case-insensitive, while Git and Linux are case-sensitive. Renaming files only by casing can leave the repo in an inconsistent state.

If git mv doesn't work (e.g. aborts), you can fix it by forcing Git to reset the index and restore the correct casing from HEAD.

1. Remove the problematic file(s)

git rm -f path/to/file

2. Restore the correct file from HEAD (with correct casing)

git checkout HEAD -- path/to/File

3. Clean untracked leftovers (preview first!)

git clean -fdn

git clean -fd

4. Commit the fix

git commit -m "fix: resolve casing issue"

Bonus ( If repo is not broken )

git mv file.js temp.js

git mv temp.js File.js

This forces all systems to recognise the change.

Q: AppBar loads with delay when using AndroidView with WebView in Jetpack Compose A:

Simply add clipToBounds() to the AndroidView's Modifier:

AndroidView(
    modifier = Modifier
        .wrapContentSize()
        .clipToBounds(),
    factory = { WebView(it) }
)

Alternatively, set clipToOutline = true on the WebView instance:

AndroidView(
    modifier = Modifier.wrapContentSize(),
    factory = { WebView(it).apply { clipToOutline = true } }
)

They're visually equivalent, but the second option will spare you a redundant GraphicsLayer underneath.

Explanation

As Mike M. seems to be explaining in basic terms in their comment above, the problem here is due to the fact that WebView is inherently unclipped. Furthermore, it draws its background color unbounded, so, if left as is, it's going to paint over anything around it drawn earlier, as far as the next outer clip or layer bounds.

You can quickly test for this issue by setting the WebView's background color to a debug value and watching for the overdraw:

AndroidView(
    factory = { context ->
        WebView(context).apply { setBackgroundColor(Color.Magenta.toArgb()) }
    },
    …
)

The easy fix, as Mike M. notes, is to clip the draw ourselves, though their description of the Modifier addition may be a little confusing if you've not seen it before:

AndroidView(
    modifier = Modifier
        .wrapContentSize()
        .graphicsLayer { clip = true },
    …
)

The clipToBounds() modifier shown at the beginning is an "alias" for exactly this, and is probably preferable if handling the clip in Compose.

Further info

As it turns out, the docs for AndroidView allude to this issue, but it's not really obvious unless you already know what's happening:

AndroidView will not clip its content to the layout bounds. Use View.setClipToOutline on the child View to clip the contents, if desired. Developers will likely want to do this with all subclasses of SurfaceView to keep its contents contained.

Any View that doesn't clip or contain its draw could potentially do the same or similar. We can demonstrate this with a plain View that does nothing more than draw an unbounded color. The example below shows just such a minimal subclass in a likewise minimal Compose setup.

As for why we've never seen this before in the native framework, all Views are clipped to their own bounds by default1, so we're very unlikely to encounter this issue there. In Compose, however, everything is unclipped by default2, which is what's allowing this behavior to surface so readily here: the AppBar draws first, then the WebView goes next and paints over everything, causing the AppBar to remain erased until it's invalidated again, either through user interaction or subsequent internal updates.

The other solutions mentioned by Mike M. and BenjyTec (here) are ultimately doing this same thing: clipping the WebView's draw, though by using an otherwise extraneous UI element to do so. We can verify this in the FrameLayout wrapper by setting its clipChildren to false, which will cause the problem to reappear. I don't think it's possible to disable the clip on a LazyColumn, unfortunately.

1. This is determined by the parent's clipChildren value. ViewGroup has that set to true by default, which is why merely wrapping the WebView fixes the issue here.

2. By "everything", I mean the base element in Compose is unclipped by default. Other Composables, including those in the core libraries, may add their own clips internally, through parameters, or possibly both.

Minimal example

The following should be tested on a device with the Run Preview option rather than in the IDE's Preview window, since that seems to invalidate things a bit differently than the actual runtime. The result will be a blank screen (not counting the action bar, if present), though the Box should obviously be visible.

import android.content.Context
import android.graphics.Canvas
import android.util.AttributeSet
import android.view.View
import androidx.compose.foundation.background
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.Box
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.Column
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.fillMaxWidth
import androidx.compose.foundation.layout.height
import androidx.compose.runtime.Composable
import androidx.compose.ui.Modifier
import androidx.compose.ui.graphics.Color
import androidx.compose.ui.tooling.preview.Preview
import androidx.compose.ui.unit.dp
import androidx.compose.ui.viewinterop.AndroidView

@Preview
@Composable
fun UnboundedDrawTest() {
    Column {
        Box(
            modifier = Modifier
                .fillMaxWidth()
                .height(200.dp)
                .background(Color.Blue)
        )
        // Substituting ::WebView works here too.
        AndroidView(factory = ::UnboundedDrawView)
    }
}

class UnboundedDrawView
@JvmOverloads constructor(
    context: Context,
    attrs: AttributeSet? = null
) : View(context, attrs) {

    override fun onDraw(canvas: Canvas) =
        canvas.drawColor(android.graphics.Color.WHITE)
}

We can use the same custom View to show that this issue is possible in the native framework as well:

<LinearLayout
    xmlns:android="http://schemas.android.com/apk/res/android"
    android:layout_width="match_parent"
    android:layout_height="match_parent"
    android:clipChildren="false"
    android:orientation="vertical">

    <View
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="200dp"
        android:background="#0000ff" />

    <com.example.app.UnboundedDrawView
        android:layout_width="match_parent"
        android:layout_height="match_parent" />

</LinearLayout>

The clipChildren="false" on the parent allows our UnboundedDrawView to paint over the blue View above it. Changing clipChildren to true, or just removing it, will contain our View and the blue one will appear.

If you build UnboundedDrawView, this example will work in the layout editor's preview, unlike WebView, which only renders when attached to a Window. If you do want to test WebView's overdraw here, make the substitution in the XML and run it normally in an Activity.

Q: Advice Regarding Full-stack Development & Beginner Freelancing A:

https://roadmap.sh/roadmaps sums it up pretty decently. Asking if you can start "today", is quite a strange question without knowing how many hours, years, have you spent in the field. If you created successfully several working and useful systems, applications, and have hundreds of other mini experiments under your belt, sure, you might be ready. Again, hard to answer properly. A bit personal but, I started after having created for fun 6 websites (and many utilities, tools, games, libraries). One day a vendor gave me a businesscard. Noticing there was no domain with a proper email and website, I just asked if they needed one. There are also many nonprofit org. that do need some sort of help as consulting or software development. Take any opportunity even if it seems a hard stretch.

Q: Why should I learn Javascript if I could just learn jQuery? A:

JQuery is Javascript. It doesn't make any sense to choose between the two. This is like saying "should I learn to cook or learn to make fried eggs?". One is a subset of the other. The same goes for Angular and Vue. You need to learn Javascript to be able to effectively use any of them.
